papers.title_in_file: Balancing Expressivity and Learnability in Quantum Kernel Bandit Optimization
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, sections 2 to 5 and Appendix L; appendix proofs skimmed only.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper on Gaussian process bandit optimization with approximated quantum kernels, with regret bounds.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in regimes where the full quantum kernel is excessively high-dimensional, they show a suitably chosen approximate kernel achieves strictly lower regret than the full model.
quotes: In regimes where the full quantum kernel is excessively high-dimensional, we show that a suitably chosen approximate kernel achieves strictly lower regret than the full model (Figure 1).
assertions.certainty_reason: Regret bounds and simulations by the authors; proofs in the appendices were not checked in this pass.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim is conditional on regimes where the full kernel is too high-dimensional.

assertions.value: The authors state that the information gain of a fidelity quantum kernel scales exponentially in the number of qubits n, and that this scaling is tight for many practical data-encoding circuits.
quotes: This scaling is exponential in the number of qubits n, and is tight for many practical data-encoding circuits
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the main text with the derivation in an appendix that was not read in this pass.

assertions.value: The authors report a U-shaped trend of regret against approximation complexity in their experiments, and that both approximation methods significantly outperform the full quantum kernel at their optimal complexity on the phase classification task.
quotes: beyond an optimal point, further increase in complexity leads to higher regret due to increased information gain, mirroring overfitting in classical learning.
Both approximation methods significantly outperform the full quantum kernel (rightmost points) at their optimal complexity.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated experiments from one study on synthetic and small physics tasks.

assertions.value: The authors state that their regret bounds may be overly conservative in practice and that their Gaussian noise model does not capture structured NISQ noise such as readout errors, depolarizing noise, relaxation, drift, or cross-talk.
quotes: Our theoretical regret bounds provide upper estimates that may be overly conservative in practice.
This abstraction does not capture structured NISQ noise, such as readout errors, depolarizing noise, relaxation, drift, or cross-talk.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limits in Appendix L.

papers.title_in_file: Noise-enhanced quantum kernels on analog quantum computers
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, sections on kernels, benchmark results, non-Markovianity results and conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study of analog and hybrid quantum kernels for regression, including the effect of simulated operational noise.

assertions.value: The authors report that the hybrid quantum kernel outperforms the RBF kernel on their benchmark dataset in numerical simulation, and describe this as supporting a potential quantum advantage on that dataset.
quotes: Furthermore, the hybrid model even outperforms the RBF model, supporting the potential quantum advantage in this dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulated benchmark in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Support for advantage is stated as potential, on a tailored dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report that operational noise can be beneficial to the performance of the analog and hybrid quantum kernels in their simulations, and attribute this to improved expressivity and higher model complexity induced by noise.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and benchmark results, pp.1 and 5
quotes: Our results reveal that the presence of operational noise can be beneficial to the performance of the developed quantum kernels.
We attribute this counterintuitive noise-enhanced performance to the improved expressivity and higher model complexity induced by noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated noise ensembles from one study; the mechanism is the authors' attribution.

assertions.value: The authors report that the noise enhancement depends on interatomic distance: in the presence of noise the analog model improves when the interatomic distances exceed Rb, whereas the hybrid model performs better when they are set below Rb.
quotes: the performance of the analog model (Fig. 5a) can be improved when the interatomic distances exceed Rb; whereas the hybrid model (Fig. 5b) performs better when the interatomic distances are set below Rb.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result limiting where noise helps.

assertions.value: The authors state that they implement the numerical simulations of the quantum kernel functions for both ideal and noisy cases with QuantumToolbox.jl.
quotes: We utilize QuantumToolbox.jl [77] to implement the numerical simulations of the quantum kernel functions for both ideal and noisy cases
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own method in the benchmark results section.
assertions.reader_inference: The results come from classical simulation, not hardware.

papers.title_in_file: Understanding Generalization in Quantum Machine Learning with Margins
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 2 (bound), section 3 experiments, conclusion; appendices skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper giving a margin-based generalization bound for quantum neural networks.

assertions.value: The paper establishes a margin-based generalization bound for quantum neural networks, and states that the bound is tighter when the hypothesis classifies the sample set with larger margins.
quotes: Unlike uniform generalization bounds, a margin bound offers a tighter upper bound when the hypothesis classifies the sample set S with larger margins.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2.1, p.3; proved in Appendix A.1.

assertions.value: The authors report that in their QCNN experiments on the quantum phase recognition dataset, margin-based metrics were better predictors of the generalization gap than parameter-based metrics in all settings, with higher mutual information and Kendall rank correlation coefficients.
quotes: In all settings, margin-based metrics proved to be better predictors of the generalization gap, showing higher mutual information and Kendall rank correlation coefficients.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated experiments from one study on one dataset family.

assertions.value: The authors report that, comparing quantum embedding methods experimentally, embeddings with higher trace distances consistently result in better generalization performance.
quotes: By comparing different quantum embedding methods, we experimentally demonstrated that embeddings with higher trace distances consistently result in better generalization performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum noise reduces trace distance between quantum states, leading to smaller classification margins and poorer generalization, and that a deeper theoretical understanding of noise, margins and generalization is left open.
quotes: A deeper theoretical understanding of the relationship between noise, margins, and generalization, along with strategies to mitigate these effects, will be critical
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as an open question in its conclusion.

papers.title_in_file: A variational quantum algorithm by Bayesian Inference with von Mises-Fisher distribution
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, sections II to IV (theorems), section V remarks; appendices skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper proposing a Bayesian, von Mises-Fisher based ground-state search for Hamiltonians, with convergence theorems and no numerical results found.

assertions.value: The paper states a theorem that at any iteration the overlap between the new mean vector and the true vector is never smaller than that of the current mean vector, and the authors state convergence is guaranteed for the whole Hilbert space and for subspaces.
assertions.anchor: Theorem 1, Section IV, p.8; Section V
quotes: Theorem 1. At any nth iteration, the overlap between the new mean vector
The convergence of the solution is not only guaranteed when searching the whole Hilbert space but also applied for the subspaces
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1, Section IV, p.8 (proof given in the text).

assertions.value: The authors state that their theoretical analysis shows the algorithm can find solutions for any Hamiltonian matrix with eigenvalues assumed within a bounded range, without requiring prior knowledge about the solution.
quotes: Our theoretical analysis has shown the capability of our algorithm in finding solutions for any Hamiltonian matrix with eigenvalues assumed within the range
without requiring any prior knowledge about the solution.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II states the eigenvalue-range assumption; Section V restates the scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that a practical algorithm is left to a forthcoming paper.
quotes: This lays the groundwork for the development of a practical algorithm which will be presented in a forthcoming paper.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit in Section V.
assertions.reader_inference: No numerical or hardware results appeared in the sections read.

papers.title_in_file: Q-SYNTH: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Adversarial Augmentation for Imbalanced Fraud Detection
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, background, method summary, results section IV, discussion and conclusion; tables read as text.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of a quantum-generator GAN that synthesizes minority-class credit card fraud samples.

assertions.value: The authors report that Q-SYNTH reduces marginal discrepancies relative to the classical GAN (KS median 0.069000 against 0.184959; Wasserstein median 0.498000 against 1.514651), and that SMOTE achieves the closest marginal agreement with real fraud samples.
assertions.anchor: Section IV fidelity results, Table III
quotes: Q-SYNTH reduces these discrepancies relative to the classical GAN across all reported marginal indicators (KS median 0.069000; Wasserstein median 0.498000; P75 1.00200)
the classical GAN exhibits substantially larger marginal discrepancies (KS median 0.184959 and Wasserstein median 1.514651)
SMOTE achieves the closest marginal agreement with real fraud samples (lowest KS and Wasserstein distances, highest KS p-value)
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one public dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report that a logistic regression detector separates real from synthetic fraud at AUC 0.475 for Q-SYNTH, 0.518764 for SMOTE and 0.51155 for the classical GAN.
assertions.anchor: Section IV fidelity results, Table III
quotes: SMOTE and GAN remain close to low detectability (AUC 0.518764 and 0.51155). Q-SYNTH yields AUC = 0.475
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that Q-SYNTH generally improves fraud recall and F1-score relative to the balanced baseline and SMOTE across the reported models, while the classical GAN attains the strongest downstream scores in several configurations.
assertions.anchor: Section IV downstream results, Table IV
quotes: Relative to the balanced baseline and to SMOTE, Q-SYNTH generally improves fraud recall and fraud F1-score across the reported models
At the same time, the classical GAN attains the strongest downstream scores in several configurations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the classical GAN is not beaten downstream.
assertions.reader_inference: Q-SYNTH does not beat the classical GAN downstream in several configurations.

assertions.value: The authors state that results are obtained within a compressed representation pipeline made to keep hybrid quantum generation tractable, and that hardware-aware evaluation under NISQ constraints remains a next step.
quotes: Third, the present results are obtained within a compressed representation pipeline designed to make hybrid quantum generation tractable for tabular fraud synthesis.
Finally, hardware-aware evaluation remains an important next step for understanding performance under realistic NISQ constraints, including noise, limited connectivity, circuit depth, and shot cost.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope and limits in the discussion.

papers.title_in_file: Compact Representation of Particle-Collision Events for Physics-Informed Machine Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, section 4 performance, section 5 quantum prospects, conclusion.
papers.what_it_is: A collider-physics ML paper compressing the rapidity-mass matrix into a 46-feature representation, with quantum compatibility argued but not run.

assertions.value: The authors report that in a supervised MLP test on simulated events the AUC is 0.998 for the full RMM and 0.999 for RMM-C46, and state that both compact representations achieve nearly the same performance while reducing dimensionality by orders of magnitude.
quotes: AUC(Full RMM) = 0.998, AUC(RMM-C46) = 0.999.
Remarkably, both compact representations achieve nearly the same performance while reducing the dimensionality by orders of magnitude.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated Monte Carlo events from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that in an autoencoder anomaly detection test the AUC is 0.9865 for the full RMM and 0.9995 for RMM-C46.
quotes: AUC(Full RMM) = 0.9865, AUC(RMM-C46) = 0.9995.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated Monte Carlo events from one study.

assertions.value: The authors claim that the compact representation is naturally compatible with near-term quantum machine-learning architectures.
quotes: Their compactness, stability, and physics transparency also make them naturally compatible with near-term quantum machine-learning architectures.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no quantum run was found in the sections read.
assertions.reader_inference: Compatibility is argued from feature count and encoding, not demonstrated on a quantum model.

assertions.value: The authors state that the compressed representation reduces kinematic information for low-momentum objects and that they expect it to perform best for events with several hard, well-separated jets, leptons, and photons.
quotes: The compressed representation reduces kinematic information for low-momentum objects. Therefore, we expect it to perform best for events containing several hard, well-separated jets, leptons, and photons.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit in Section 5.1.

papers.title_in_file: SantaQlaus: A resource-efficient method to leverage quantum shot-noise for optimization of variational quantum algorithms
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, framework overview, section V numerical simulations and section VI conclusion; derivations skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: An optimizer for variational quantum algorithms that anneals the number of measurement shots, tested in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that numerical simulations on VQE and QML tasks show SantaQlaus outperforming existing optimizers, particularly in mitigating convergence to poor local optima, while maintaining shot efficiency.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Section V, pp.1 and 13-17
quotes: Numerical simulations on VQE and QML demonstrate that SantaQlaus outperforms existing optimizers, particularly in mitigating the risks of converging to poor local optima
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated benchmarks from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that on an Iris classification task with simulated local depolarizing noise, SantaQlaus maintains nearly consistent performance under the noise while the noise significantly impairs the Adam-DS optimizer.
quotes: In contrast, SantaQlaus maintains nearly consistent performance levels under the same noise.
Indeed, the presence of hardware noise significantly impairs the learning performance of the Adam-DS optimizer.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated noise on one small dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main benchmarks do not include hardware noise, that the Iris task adds local depolarizing noise, and that additional research is needed to assess performance in experiments.
assertions.anchor: Section V p.13, Section V.C p.16, Section VI p.17
quotes: We do not include hardware noise.
In this simulation, hardware noise is incorporated, specifically modeled as local depolarizing noise.
Looking ahead, additional research is needed to assess performance of SantaQlaus in experiments.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own simulation scope and limit.
assertions.reader_inference: No run on quantum hardware is reported.

papers.title_in_file: Provable and scalable quantum Gaussian processes for quantum learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results, discussion, methods proof sketch; supplementary proofs located and sampled only.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper showing matchgate evolutions yield Gaussian processes over quantum data, with classical-simulation demonstrations.

assertions.value: The paper proves that matchgate (free-fermionic) evolutions give rise to provable and scalable quantum Gaussian processes, the first family in its framework where the unknown unitary acts non-trivially on all qubits.
quotes: We then prove that matchgate, or free-fermionic, evolutions give rise to provable and scalable quantum Gaussian processes, providing the first family in our framework where the unknown unitary acts non-trivially on all qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 (informal statement p.5; formal proof in the Supplementary Information).

assertions.value: The authors state that Theorem 1 guarantees the provable QGP condition but that scalability is not automatic, and that efficient polynomial scaling in the total number of qubits n requires the kernel entries to stay of the same order as those in the noise covariance R.
quotes: Theorem 1 guarantees the provable QGP condition, but scalability is not automatic.
Consequently, to achieve efficient polynomial scaling in the total number of qubits n while ensuring that the kernel entries remain of the same order as those in R
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit of the theorem, p.5.

assertions.value: The authors report a 50-qubit regression task, trained on 15 points, in which a quantum Gaussian process with the correct matchgate inductive bias extrapolates, and that extrapolation becomes impossible without a suitable inductive bias.
quotes: We consider a 50-qubit regression task where the model is trained on 15 points in the interval

Thus, the first example shows that successful interpolation can generally be achieved, here with only 15 training points in a narrow region, but extrapolation becomes impossible in the absence of a suitable inductive bias.
assertions.certainty_reason: Classical simulation of a matchgate task in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Matchgate circuits are classically simulable, so the demonstration does not show a quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The paper states that Gaussian states combined with Pauli observables in B4 cannot lead to GPs, a consequence of Theorem 2.
quotes: This violation implies, as per Theorem 2, that Gaussian states combined with Pauli observables in B4 cannot lead to GPs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2 and Theorems C.3 and C.4 in the Supplementary Information.
